## Central Limit Theorem (CLT)
```{r clt}
#| cache: true

# 1. GENERATE SHAPES DATA
set.seed(42)

# --- Top: Skewed Population ---
# Generate skewed data and density
pop_dist = rbeta(10000, 2, 5) 
d_pop = density(pop_dist)
# Scale density to fit in the top part of the plot (Y: 7.5 to 9.5)
df_pop = tibble(x = d_pop$x, y = d_pop$y)
df_pop$x_scaled = scales::rescale(df_pop$x, to = c(2, 8)) # Center horizontally
df_pop$y_scaled = scales::rescale(df_pop$y, to = c(7.5, 9.5)) # Top vertical position

# --- Bottom: Normal Sampling Distribution ---
# Generate normal data and density
norm_dist = rnorm(10000)
d_norm = density(norm_dist)
# Scale density to fit in bottom part (Y: 0.5 to 2.5)
df_norm = data.frame(x = d_norm$x, y = d_norm$y)
df_norm$x_scaled = scales::rescale(df_norm$x, to = c(3, 7)) # Center, narrower
df_norm$y_scaled = scales::rescale(df_norm$y, to = c(0.5, 2.5)) # Bottom vertical position

# --- Middle: Sample Buckets ---
# Coordinates for 3 sample boxes
samples_df = tibble(
  id = c("Sample 1", "Sample 2", "Sample 3"),
  x_center = c(2.5, 5, 7.5),
  y_center = rep(5, 3),
  width = 1.2,
  height = 1.2
)

# Random dots for inside the buckets
dots_df = samples_df %>% 
  rowwise() %>% 
  mutate(
    dots_x = list(runif(10, x_center - width/2.5, x_center + width/2.5)),
    dots_y = list(runif(10, y_center - height/2.5, y_center + height/2.5))
  ) %>% 
  unnest(cols = c(dots_x, dots_y))

# 2. PLOT
clt_plot = ggplot() +
  # --- TOP LAYER: POPULATION ---
  geom_polygon(data = df_pop, aes(x = x_scaled, y = y_scaled), 
               fill = "black", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 2, y = 9), label = "Population\nDistribution", 
            hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5, fontface = "bold", size = 6, color = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(x = 8.2, y = 8.5), label = "(Unknown,\npotenially skewed)", 
            hjust = 0, vjust = 0.5, size = 5, color = "grey40", fontface = "italic") +

  # --- MIDDLE LAYER: SAMPLES ---
  # Draw rectangles for buckets
  geom_tile(data = samples_df, aes(x = x_center, y = y_center, width = width, height = height),
            fill = "#f6f5f3", color = "#E69F00", linewidth = 1.5) +
  # Add dots inside
  geom_point(data = dots_df, aes(x = dots_x, y = dots_y), 
             color = "#E69F00", size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_text(data = samples_df, aes(x = x_center, y = y_center - 0.9, label = id),
            size = 5, fontface = "bold", color = "#E69F00") +
  
  # --- BOTTOM LAYER: SAMPLING DIST ---
  geom_polygon(data = df_norm, aes(x = x_scaled, y = y_scaled), 
               fill = "#CC79A7", alpha = 0.6) +
   geom_text(aes(x = 2, y = 1.5), label = "Sampling\nDistribution", 
            hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5, fontface = "bold", size = 6, color = "#CC79A7") +
  geom_text(aes(x = 7.2, y = 1.5), label = "(Normal,\npredictable!)", 
            hjust = 0, vjust = 0.5, size = 5, color = "#CC79A7", fontface = "italic") +

  # --- ARROWS ---
  # Arrows Down from Pop to Samples
  geom_curve(aes(x = 5, y = 7.5, xend = 2.5, yend = 5.7), 
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")), curvature = 0.2, color = "grey60") +
  geom_curve(aes(x = 5, y = 7.5, xend = 5, yend = 5.7), 
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")), curvature = 0, color = "grey60") +
  geom_curve(aes(x = 5, y = 7.5, xend = 7.5, yend = 5.7), 
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")), curvature = -0.2, color = "grey60") +
  
  # Arrows Converging to Sampling Dist
  geom_curve(aes(x = 2.5, y = 4.3, xend = 5, yend = 2.6), 
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")), curvature = -0.2, color = "grey60") +
  geom_curve(aes(x = 5, y = 4.3, xend = 5, yend = 2.6), 
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")), curvature = 0, color = "grey60") +
  geom_curve(aes(x = 7.5, y = 4.3, xend = 5, yend = 2.6), 
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")), curvature = 0.2, color = "grey60") +

  # --- THEME ---
  xlim(0, 10) + ylim(0, 10) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#f6f5f3", color = NA))
clt_plot
```

## Motivating questions 

<div style="font-size: 150%;">

::: {.incremental}

+ How much protein do Americans consume, on average? 

+ Has protein consumption changed in the last 20 years? 

+ We will use the CLT  to help us answer these questions


</div>

:::

---


## First, definitions 

::: {.incremental}

<div style="font-size: 150%;">

+ Mean: average, center of data

+ Standard deviation (SD): measure of spread of data; average squared distance from mean

+ (Probability) distribution: mathematically describes possible values for a variable and how often they occur

</div>
:::

---

## The Normal Distribution (bell curve) 


```{r normal dist}
#| cache: true 


p_normal = 
  ggplot(data = tibble(x = c(-3.2, 3.2)), aes(x)) +
  geom_area(stat = "function", fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1), 
            xlim = c(-3.2, 3.2), fill = "#56B4E9", alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, n = 101, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1), linewidth = 1.1) +
  # theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())+
  labs(y = "Density", x = "Data (x)") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-3, 3, 1))

p_normal 
```

## What's special about the Normal distribution? 

::: {.incremental}

<div style="font-size: 150%;">

+ Symmetric 
+ Described by two parameters: mean and standard deviation 
+ 68-95-99.7 rule tells us where most of data lie 
+ We can calculate probabilities of values occurring within the distribution

</div>
:::

---


### Mean: shifts left/right

```{r pmeans}
#| cache: true 

p_means = 
  ggplot(data = tibble(x = c(-4.2, 4.2)), aes(x)) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, n = 101, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1), linewidth = 1.1, aes(color = "Mean = 0")) +
    stat_function(fun = dnorm, n = 101, args = list(mean = 1, sd = 1), linewidth = 1.1, aes(color = "Mean = 1")) +
      stat_function(fun = dnorm, n = 101, args = list(mean = -1, sd = 1), linewidth = 1.1, aes(color = "Mean = -1")) +
  # theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())+
  labs(y = "Density", x = "Data (x)", title = "Normal Distributions with Different Means") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-4, 4, 1)) +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.9, 0.9),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 14),
        legend.background = element_rect(fill="#f6f5f3", color = "darkgrey"),
        legend.title = element_blank(),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 14)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#009E73", "#000000", "#D55E00"), name = "")
p_means

```

### Standard Deviation: controls spread

```{r sd}
#| cache: true


p_sds = 
  ggplot(data = tibble(x = c(-4.5, 4.5)), aes(x)) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, n = 101, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 0.5), linewidth = 1.1, aes(color = "SD = 0.5")) +
    stat_function(fun = dnorm, n = 101, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1), linewidth = 1.1, aes(color = "SD = 1")) +
      stat_function(fun = dnorm, n = 101, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 2), linewidth = 1.1, aes(color = "SD = 2")) +
  labs(y = "Density", x = "Data (x)", title = "Normal Distributions with Different Standard Deviations") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-4, 4, 1)) +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.9, 0.9),
        legend.background = element_rect(fill="#f6f5f3",color = "darkgrey"),
        legend.title = element_blank(),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 14)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#000000", "#CC79A7"), name = "")

p_sds
```

### 68-95-99.7 Rule

```{r normal again mean}
#| cache: true 
ggplot(data = tibble(x = c(-3.2, 3.2)), aes(x)) +
  # theme(axis.text.y = element_blank()) +
  labs(y = "Density", x = "Data (x)") +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, n = 201, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1),
                linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-3, 3, 1)) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 0), linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate(geom = "label", x = 0, y = 0.35, label = "Mean = 0", size = 8) 
  



```

---

### 68-95-99.7 Rule

```{r normal1}
#| cache: true 

shade_df1 = tibble(
  x = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 500),
  y = dnorm(seq(-1, 1, length.out = 500), mean = 0, sd = 1)
)

shade_df2 = tibble(
  x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 500),
  y = dnorm(seq(-2, 2, length.out = 500), mean = 0, sd = 1)
)

shade_df3 = tibble(
  x = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 500),
  y = dnorm(seq(-3, 3, length.out = 500), mean = 0, sd = 1)
)

pn_1 = ggplot(data = tibble(x = c(-3.2, 3.2)), aes(x)) +
  geom_area(data = shade_df1, aes(x = x, y = y),
            fill = "#E69F00", alpha = 0.5) +
  annotate(geom = "label",
           x = 0, y = 0.3, color = "#E69F00",
           label = "68% of data",size = 8) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, n = 201, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1),
                linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate(geom = "segment", x = 1, xend = 1,
           y = 0, yend= shade_df1$y[shade_df1$x==1],
           linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate(geom = "label", x = 1, y = 0.15, label = "Mean + 1 SD", size = 5) +
   annotate(geom = "segment", x = -1, xend = -1,
           y = 0, yend= shade_df1$y[shade_df1$x==-1],
           linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate(geom = "label", x = -1, y = 0.15, label = "Mean - 1 SD", size = 5) +
  # theme(axis.text.y = element_blank()) +
  labs(y = "Density", x = "Data (x)") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-3, 3, 1))


pn_1 
```

### SAT Scores 

```{r sat again}
#| cache: true 


sat_df = 
  sat_score %>% 
  as_tibble()  
sat_mean = mean(sat_df$value)
sat_sd = sd(sat_df$value)  


dens = density(sat_score)
dens_df = tibble(x = dens$x, y = dens$y) %>% 
  mutate(y = y *  nrow(sat_df) * 50)

x = seq(min(sat_score), max(sat_score), 1)
dens_df = tibble(x= x, y = dnorm(x, mean = mean(sat_df$value), sd = sd(sat_df$value)) * nrow(sat_df) * 50)


sat_df %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  labs(x = "SAT Score", y = "Count of students", title = "SAT Scores among US high school students",
       subtitle = glue::glue("2017: 95% of scores between ", round(sat_mean - 2*sat_sd), " and ",
                             round(sat_mean + 2*sat_sd))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma, limits = c(0, 190000)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(400, 1600,100))+
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(count)), 
                 color = "black", fill = "#56B4E9",  binwidth = 50) +
  stat_function(
    fun = function(x) dnorm(x, mean = mean(sat_df$value), sd = sd(sat_df$value)) * nrow(sat_df) * 50,
    linewidth = 1.3,
    color = "#E69F00"
  ) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = sat_mean), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = sat_mean + 2*sat_sd), linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = sat_mean - 2*sat_sd), linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate(geom = "label", x = sat_mean + 2*sat_sd, y = 150000,
           label = glue::glue("Mean + 2 SD\n", round(sat_mean+2*sat_sd, 0)), size = 4) +
  annotate(geom = "label", x = sat_mean - 2*sat_sd, y = 150000,
           label = glue::glue("Mean - 2 SD\n", round(sat_mean-2*sat_sd, 0)), size = 4) +
  geom_area(data = dens_df %>% filter(x <= sat_mean + 2*sat_sd & x >= sat_mean - 2*sat_sd),
            aes(x, y = y), alpha = 0.5, inherit.aes = F,
            fill = "#E69F00") +
  annotate(geom = "label", x = sat_mean, y = 160000,
           label = glue::glue("Mean\n", round(sat_mean, 0)), size = 4) 

```

### Weight 

```{r weight}
#| cache: true 

pdens= 
  bmx_joined %>% 
  filter(age_in_years_at_screening >= 18) %>% 
  mutate(weight_lbs = weight_kg * 2.2) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = weight_lbs, color = gender, fill = gender)) + 
  facet_wrap(.~gender, scales = "free") +
```

## The problem

::: {.incremental}
<div style="font-size: 150%;">

+ Normally distributed data is easy to work with
+ Most data isn't Normally distributed
+ It turns out that the **averages** of non-Normal data are Normal 

</div> 

:::

::: {.incremental}

+ Imagine we know the hours worked for every adult in the U.S. This is the **population**

+ We saw before that this data is not Normal

+ Now let's pretend we *don't* have data on every person, we just have a random selection of 50 people from that population. This is a **sample**

+ What does the distribution of the samples look like?

# What does the distribution of these sample means look like? 

---


### Sampling distribution: income data 

```{ojs}
data2 = FileAttachment("work_df.csv").csv({ typed: true })

viewof sample_size2 = Inputs.range(
  [2, 100], 
  {value: 30, step: 1, label: "Sample size:"}
)

//viewof n_samples = Inputs.range(
//  [10, 1000], 
  //{value: 500, step: 10, label: "Number samples:"}
//)

sample_means2 = {
  // Dependency tracking: re-run when these change
  sample_size2;
  
  // Safety check: ensure data is loaded
  if (!data2 || data2.length === 0) return [];
  
  // Safety check: ensure column exists (Case Sensitive!)
  if (typeof data2[0].hrs_worked === "undefined") {
    return ["Error: Column 'hrs_worked' not found in data"];
  }

  const means = [];
  // Create a local copy of the array to shuffle
  // We do this inside the loop or use a specific shuffler to ensure 
  // we are sampling from the full population every time.
  const popArray = Array.from(data2); 

  for (let i = 0; i < 500; i++) {
    // 1. Shuffle a clean copy of the population
    // 2. Slice the first n elements (Sampling WITHOUT replacement)
    const sample = d3.shuffle([...popArray]).slice(0, sample_size2);

    // 3. Compute mean
    const m = d3.mean(sample, d => d.hrs_worked);
    means.push(m);
  }

  return means;
}


// 5. CALCULATE NORMAL CURVE (THEORETICAL)
// We now generate the curve based on the Population Parameters, not the sample.
// This shows the Theoretical prediction of the CLT.
normalCurve2 = {
  if (sample_means2.length < 2 || !data2) return [];
  
  // 1. Get Population Statistics
  const popMean = d3.mean(data2, d => d.hrs_worked);
  const popSD = d3.deviation(data2, d => d.hrs_worked);
  
  // 2. Calculate Standard Error (The predicted width of the sampling distribution)
  // Formula: Population SD / sqrt(n)
  const se = popSD / Math.sqrt(sample_size2);

  // 3. Determine range for the curve (centered on popMean)
  const minX = popMean - (4 * se);
  const maxX = popMean + (4 * se);
  
  // Create a smooth grid of X values
  const grid = d3.range(minX, maxX, (maxX - minX) / 200);
  
  // Normal Density Function using Population Mean and Standard Error
  const pdf = (x) => (1 / (se * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI))) * Math.exp(-0.5 * Math.pow((x - popMean) / se, 2));
  
  return grid.map(x => ({x: x, y: pdf(x)}));
}

// 6. PLOT
// 6. SIDE-BY-SIDE PLOTS WITH EXTERNAL LEGEND
{
  // --- A. SETUP VARIABLES ---
  const popMean = d3.mean(data2, d => d.hrs_worked);
  const n = sample_means2.length;
  const bins = d3.bin().thresholds(20)(sample_means2);
  
  // NEW: Calculate fixed x-axis limits based on the Population Data
  // This ensures the axis stays constant regardless of sample size
  const xLimits = d3.extent(data2, d => d.hrs_worked);

  // Define colors
  const colorDomain = ["Sample Mean", "Population Mean", "Normal Curve"];
  const colorRange = ["#D55E00", "black", "#CC79A7"];

  // --- B. POPULATION PLOT (Left) ---
  const popPlot = Plot.plot({
    width: 550,
    height: 500,
    caption: "Population Distribution (Raw Data)",
    marginTop: 40,
    marginLeft: 50,
    marginBottom: 40,
    style: { fontSize: "14px", overflow: "visible" },
    
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(data2, Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: "hrs_worked", fill: "#E69F00", fillOpacity: 0.5})),
    ],
    // We explicitly set the domain here too, just to be safe and consistent
    x: { label: "Hours worked", domain: xLimits }, 
    y: { label: "Count" }
  });

  // --- C. SAMPLING DISTRIBUTION PLOT (Right) ---
  const sampPlot = Plot.plot({
    width: 550,
    height: 500,
    caption: `Sampling Distribution (n=${sample_size2})`,
    marginTop: 40,
    marginLeft: 50,
    marginBottom: 40,
    style: { fontSize: "14px", overflow: "visible" },
    
    color: {
      domain: colorDomain,
      range: colorRange,
      legend: false
    },
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(bins, {
        x1: "x0", x2: "x1", 
        y: d => d.length / (n * (d.x1 - d.x0)), 
        fill: "#56B4E9", fillOpacity: 0.5, tip: true,
        title: d => `Count: ${d.length}\nDensity: ${(d.length / (n * (d.x1 - d.x0))).toFixed(3)}`
      }),
      Plot.line(normalCurve2, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: () => "Normal Curve", strokeWidth: 3}),
      Plot.ruleX([d3.mean(sample_means2)], {stroke: () => "Sample Mean", strokeWidth: 3}),
      Plot.ruleX([popMean], {stroke: () => "Population Mean", strokeDasharray: "4,4", strokeWidth: 2, opacity: 0.8})
    ],
    // NEW: Apply the fixed population domain here
    x: { label: "Sample Mean", tickFormat: ".1f", domain: xLimits }, 
    y: { label: "Density" }
  });

  // --- D. LEGEND & LAYOUT ---
  const myLegend = Plot.legend({
    color: { domain: colorDomain, range: colorRange },
    style: { marginBottom: "10px", fontSize: "14px" }
  });

  return html`
  <div style="display: flex; flex-direction: column; align-items: center;">
    <div style="width: 100%; max-width: 920px; display: flex; justify-content: flex-end;">
      ${myLegend}
    </div>
    <div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 20px; justify-content: center;">
      <div>${popPlot}</div>
      <div>${sampPlot}</div>
    </div>
  </div>`;
}
```

Other helpful interactives: [Stats calculators](https://www.statscalculators.com/resources/simulations/central-limit-theorem), [Seeing theory](https://seeing-theory.brown.edu/probability-distributions/index.html)

---


## Central Limit Theorem

::: {.incremental}
<div style="font-size: 150%;">


+ The distribution of the sample means is approximately Normal, regardless of the shape of the population distribution, as long as the sample size is big enough !!!

  + Mean: population mean
  + SD: population SD / $\sqrt{n}$

+ What's big enough? 
  + For many distributions, $n=30$ is sufficient, but for some distributions, a larger sample size may be required

</div>

:::

---

## So what? 

::: {.incremental}

<div style="font-size: 150%;">


+ Usually, all we have is a sample (not population values)
+ From CLT, we know the distribution of the sample mean, regardless of the distribution in the population
+ We can then use this sampling distribution to learn about the population

</div>

::: 

---

## A brief history 


::: {.incremental}

<div style="font-size: 115%;">

+ **1733**: Abraham de Moivre realizes that if you flip a coin enough times, the distribution of the number of heads looks like a Normal distribution^[[https://www.jstor.org/stable/2334818?seq=1#page_scan_tab_contents](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2334818?seq=1#page_scan_tab_contents)]

+ **1812**: Pierre-Simon Laplace resurrects the idea, showing that you can approximate the Binomial distribution with a Normal distribution^[[https://archive.org/details/theorieanaldepro00laplrich](https://archive.org/details/theorieanaldepro00laplrich)]

+ **1901**: Aleksandr Lyapunov provides the first rigorous proof of the CLT^[[https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00207179208934258](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00207179208934258)] 

+ **1920s**: George Pólya first uses the term *Central Limit Theorem*^[[https://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/id/PPN266833020_0008](https://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/id/PPN266833020_0008)]

</div>
:::


---

## Application: how much protein do Americans eat, on average? 

::: {.incremental}
<div style="font-size: 115%;">


+ Data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey in 2021-2023^[[https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/continuousnhanes/default.aspx?Cycle=2021-2023](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/continuousnhanes/default.aspx?Cycle=2021-2023)]

+ There are `r nrow(protein_df23)` individuals whose protein intake was estimated from a dietary survey
  + Mean: `r round(mean(protein_df23$protein_gm), 1)` grams per day
  + SD: `r round(sd(protein_df23$protein_gm), 1)` grams per day

+ We treat these individuals as a sample^[We will revisit this later] from the population (all Americans) 

+ What is the distribution of the sample mean? 
  + Mean = ?
  + SD = ?

+ We can use the CLT to estimate the average in the population, and provide a range of plausible values for that estimate 
</div>

:::
 

---

### How much protein do Americans eat, on average?

```{r app1}
#| cache: true

protein_mean = mean(protein_df23$protein_gm)
protein_sd = sd(protein_df23$protein_gm)
protein_n = nrow(protein_df23)
protein_se = protein_sd / sqrt(protein_n)
q025 = protein_mean - 1.96 * protein_se
q975 = protein_mean + 1.96 * protein_se

# create a grid for plotting the curve
grid = tibble(x = seq(protein_mean - 4*protein_se, protein_mean + 4*protein_se, length.out=200))

# Plot the theoretical Normal curve directly
p1 = ggplot(grid, aes(x=x)) + 
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = protein_mean, sd = protein_se),
                color = "#56B4E9", linewidth = 1.1) +
  labs(x = "Protein intake (g)", y = "Density", title = "Theoretical distribution of sample mean") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = protein_mean), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = protein_mean),linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate(geom="label",
           x = protein_mean, y = 0.65,
           label=glue::glue("Mean = {round(protein_mean,1)} g"), size=5) +
  annotate(geom = "label",
           x = protein_mean,
           y = 0.25,
           label = glue::glue("SD = {round(protein_sd, 1)} / sqrt({protein_n}) = {round(protein_se, 2)} g"), size = 5,
           hjust = 0) +
  annotate(geom = "segment", 
           x = 75, xend = protein_mean, y = 0.3, yend = 0.3,
          arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.1, "inches"), type = "closed")) +
  annotate(geom = "segment", 
           x = 75, xend = protein_mean + protein_se, y = 0.3, yend = 0.3,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.1, "inches"), type = "closed")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(70, 80, 0.5))

p1
# If we think about all the sample means we could have gotten by sampling repeatedly, that forms a bell-shaped curve centered at `r round(sample_mean, 1)`, with standard deviation equal to the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size
```

## Application: has protein consumption changed?


::: {.incremental}

<div style="font-size: 115%;">

+ Has protein intake among Americans has changed from 2001 to 2023?
+ We have two samples from the population 
  + NHANES data from 2001^[[https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/continuousnhanes/default.aspx?BeginYear=2001](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/continuousnhanes/default.aspx?BeginYear=2001)] (mean: `r round(mean(protein_df01$protein_gm), 1)`)
  + NHANES data from 2023 (mean: `r round(protein_mean, 1)`)
+ We know the sample means are approximately Normally distributed 
  + It turns out that the **difference** in sample means is also Normally distributed 
  + Mean: difference in population means 
  + SD: square root of sum of variances in each sampling distribution 
+ So we can use the CLT! 

</div>
::: 

--- 


### Has protein consumption changed since 2001? 


```{r diff1}
#| cache: true 

mean01 = protein_df01$protein_gm %>% mean
sd01 = protein_df01$protein_gm %>% sd
n01 = protein_df01$protein_gm %>% length
se01 = sd01 / sqrt(n01)


grid = tibble(x = seq(min(mean01, protein_mean) - 5*protein_se, max(mean01, protein_mean) + 5*protein_se, length.out=200))


p1a =
  ggplot(grid, aes(x=x)) + 
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = protein_mean, sd = protein_se),
                aes(color = "2023",fill ="2023"), linewidth = 1.1) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mean01, sd = se01),
                aes(color = "2001",fill ="2021"), linewidth = 1.1) +
  labs(x = "Protein intake (g)", y = "Density", title = "Theoretical distribution of sample means") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = protein_mean), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean01),linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate(geom="label",
           x = protein_mean, y = 0.65,
           label=glue::glue("Mean = {round(protein_mean,1)} g"), size=5,color="#56B4E9") +
  annotate(geom="label",
           x = mean01, y = 0.7,
           label=glue::glue("Mean = {round(mean01,1)} g"), size=5,color="#CC79A7") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#CC79A7", "#56B4E9"), name = "Year") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.text = element_text(size=14),
        legend.title = element_text(size=14)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(72,82, 1)) 
p1a
```

### Has protein consumption changed since 2001? 

```{r diff2}
#| cache: true 

sddiff = sqrt((protein_sd^2 / protein_n) + (sd01^2 / n01))
difference = protein_mean - mean01


q025 = difference - 1.96 * sddiff
q975 = difference + 1.96 * sddiff

# create a grid for plotting the curve
grid = tibble(x = seq(difference - 4*sddiff, difference + 4*sddiff, length.out=200))


pdiff = ggplot(grid, aes(x=x)) + 
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = difference, sd = sddiff),
                color = "#009E73", linewidth = 1.1) +
  labs(x = "Protein intake (g)", y = "Density", title = "Theoretical distribution of difference in sample means") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = difference), linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate(geom="label",
           x = difference, y = 0.45,
           label=glue::glue("Observed difference = {round(difference,1)} g"), size=5) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 0),linetype = "dotted") 

pdiff
```

### Has protein consumption changed since 2001?

<div style="font-size: 150%;">


+ We have strong evidence that protein intake has decreased an average of ~5g since 2001
 
+ Does it mean anything? 

+ 7g of protein = 1 egg, 1 cup milk, 1/4 cup nuts 
 

+ **Statistical vs. clinical significance**

</div>
:::

---


## When does the CLT fail? 


::: {.incremental}

<div style="font-size: 115%;">

+ **Independence Violation**
  + If data are correlated (e.g., family members, time-series data), the spread of the data is not the same as predicted by the CLT 
  + *NHANES Caveat:* Real survey data is not collected randomly and is correlated, requires adjustment using survey methodology 
+ **Sample Size vs. Skew**
  + $n=30$ is a rule of thumb. Heavily skewed data requires larger $n$.
+ **Infinite Variance**
  + Theoretical limitations (e.g., Cauchy distribution) where the CLT never applies.
  
</div>

:::


## Sir Francis Galton on the CLT: 

<div style="font-size: 150%;">


"The law would have been personified by the Greeks and deified, if they had known of it. It reigns with serenity and in complete self-effacement, amidst the wildest confusion. The huger the mob, and the greater the apparent anarchy, the more perfect is its sway. It is the supreme law of Unreason. Whenever a large sample of chaotic elements are taken in hand and marshalled in the order of their magnitude, an unsuspected and most beautiful form of regularity proves to have been latent all along."^[[https://galton.org/cgi-bin/searchImages/galton/search/books/natural-inheritance/pages/natural-inheritance_0073.htm](https://galton.org/cgi-bin/searchImages/galton/search/books/natural-inheritance/pages/natural-inheritance_0073.htm)]


</div>
